readingInstruction: Read Psalm 147:1-11. You read all of Psalm 147 on Day 508 as a song for the rebuilt wall. Today read only the first eleven verses, and let them sit beside what Jesus does in the next chapters: healing the brokenhearted and binding up wounds.
settingTheScene: The first half of Psalm 147 pairs two pictures: God the builder and gatherer, and God the healer. It also tells us what pleases him. Read these verses today with the Gospel of Matthew open in your mind, where the Messiah begins to touch lepers, lift the paralyzed, and call the weary to himself.
observation: “Praise the LORD! For it is good to sing praises to our God” (v. 1).
“The LORD builds up Jerusalem; he gathers the outcasts of Israel” (v. 2).
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (v. 3).
“He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names” (v. 4).
“Great is our Lord, and abundant in power; his understanding is beyond measure” (v. 5).
“The LORD lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground” (v. 6).
“He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (v. 9).
“But the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love” (v. 11).
interpretation:
On Day 508, you heard this psalm at the dedication of the wall. Today, notice what stands out about verse 3: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” Right after the gathering of the outcasts, the psalm turns to the personal. God does not only manage nations. He kneels to bandage individual hurts.

The next verse sets this beside the stars. The same God who counts and names the stars is the one who tends the brokenhearted. His power and his tenderness are not in competition. The Gospel of Matthew gives this a face. In the chapters you are about to read, Jesus touches a leper, raises a girl, and heals the sick. Matthew says that this fulfilled what Isaiah said: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” The God of the stars came near to the broken.

Verses 10 and 11 tell us what God values. He does not delight in the strength of the horse or the legs of a man, which means military might and human physical power. He takes pleasure in those who fear him and hope in his steadfast love. God is not impressed by what we can do. He is moved by trust.

For a person who is hurting, this psalm is an invitation. You do not have to fix yourself before you come. The LORD heals the brokenhearted, and he does it because that is who he is.
connection: Matthew 8:16-17 quotes Isaiah 53:4 about Jesus healing the sick. Matthew 11:28 calls the weary and burdened to come. Luke 4:18 says he has been sent to bind up the brokenhearted. Isaiah 61:1 is the source of that verse. Psalm 34:18 says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted. 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 calls God the Father of mercies and God of all comfort. Revelation 21:4 promises that he will wipe away every tear.
application:
Name one hurt you have been carrying. Bring it to the Lord in prayer without trying to tidy it first.

Look for someone brokenhearted near you and offer a quiet act of care: a call, a note, a meal.

Tonight, look at the stars and remember that the one who named them knows your name.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.
Tell him what is broken in you.
Praise him for the stars he counts and names.
